interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through what happens between your backend sending a push and a user seeing it.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It's a three-hop pipeline, and each hop is a separate point of failure that a naive mental model of "I sent a push" glosses over.

First, your server calls the platform push service's API — Firebase Cloud Messaging for Android, APNs for iOS — with the device's registration token and a payload. That call can fail for ordinary reasons: bad credentials, a malformed payload, a stale token from a reinstalled app. Second, the push service — which maintains the actual persistent, low-power connection to the device, something your own server never has — forwards the message. This hop is best-effort by design: under load, the service can coalesce multiple pending messages into showing just the latest, or drop messages entirely if the device has been offline past its retry window. Third, the device OS decides whether to actually display it, and things like Do Not Disturb, revoked notification permission, or aggressive battery-saver states can suppress it even after it arrives.

When a user taps the notification, the OS launches or resumes the app and hands it the payload, and the app is responsible for turning that payload into actual navigation — a deep link into the relevant screen.

The practical consequence: "the push didn't arrive" can't be diagnosed from one side alone. You need your server's send confirmation, the push service's delivery status, and ideally the device's own receive event, to know which of the three hops actually failed.

**Testing:** whether you understand push as a multi-system pipeline with real failure points, rather than a single black-box "send notification" action.

interviewQuestions.question: A chat feature is losing messages for some users — they show up late or not at all, but only on some devices. How would you debug this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the hypothesis that this is push's best-effort delivery model showing up as a real bug, because "some devices, intermittently" is exactly the signature of a design that implicitly assumed push guarantees delivery.

First I'd check the architecture: is a new message's arrival on the recipient's device driven **purely** by receiving a push, with no independent sync path? If so, that's the root cause candidate — any dropped, coalesced, or delayed push under weak connectivity, power-saving states, or a push-service disruption becomes permanent message loss with nothing else to catch it.

I'd confirm by checking whether affected devices correlate with weak network conditions, low-battery/power-saving states, or the OS having recently coalesced multiple rapid pushes for that device into showing only the latest — all signatures of push being deprioritized rather than a code bug.

The fix isn't trying to make push more reliable — that's fighting the platform's own design goals. It's adding a real sync path: on app foreground, and ideally on a periodic background interval, the client asks the backend directly "what have I missed since message ID X," using push only as a low-latency wake-up hint rather than the actual transport. This is the standard pattern in production messaging apps for exactly this reason — push gets you speed when it works, sync gets you correctness always.

**Testing:** whether you can trace an intermittent production symptom back to an architectural gap (no fallback sync) rather than treating it as a one-off bug to patch.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you design the permission-request flow for notifications to maximize genuine opt-in, not just prompt acceptance?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd separate "getting the user to tap allow" from "getting the user to actually want notifications," because optimizing only for the first metric produces a worse long-term outcome — a user who taps allow without understanding why will mute or disable notifications later anyway, and a denial on the real OS prompt is close to unrecoverable without the user manually visiting settings.

The approach: never trigger the OS permission dialog cold, on first launch, before the user has any context. Instead, build a soft-ask moment tied to a concrete value the user just experienced — right after they place an order, offer "get notified when it ships" with your own in-app UI. If they opt in there, immediately follow with the real OS prompt, because a user who just said yes to your explanation is far more likely to also grant the system prompt. If they decline the soft-ask, I don't trigger the OS prompt at all — I've preserved that one shot for a better moment later, rather than burning it on a context the user wasn't ready for.

I'd also track opt-in rate segmented by *which* soft-ask moment triggered it, because different trigger points convert very differently — a soft-ask right after a relevant action reliably beats one shown at a generic settings screen or onboarding step, and that data should drive where else in the app to add similar moments.

The metric I'd actually care about isn't raw opt-in percentage — it's opt-in that survives 30 days without the user disabling notifications afterward, since that's the signal the ask happened at a moment the user genuinely valued, not just tolerated.

**Testing:** whether you think about permission requests as a product/UX design problem with measurable long-term outcomes, not just a one-time API call to get right.

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, what would you require of any new feature that adds a deep-linkable screen, before approving it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame the review around one question: **can this screen be entered cold, with zero prior in-app state, and still work correctly?** Most deep-link bugs come from a screen quietly depending on something a normal navigation path always happened to set up, and a deep link skips that path entirely.

Concretely I'd ask: does this screen fetch or reconstruct everything it needs directly, rather than assuming a predecessor screen already populated a shared view model or cache? Is the deep link's structure validated against an allowlist before acting on it, rather than trusting whatever URI arrives? And critically — does entering this screen via deep link re-check authorization server-side for whatever resource it references, so a link to `/order/12345` can't bypass the normal "does this user own order 12345" check just because it arrived as a link instead of a tap inside the app?

I'd also want to see it actually tested via a simulated deep link — not just via in-app navigation — because internal QA almost never reaches a screen this way by accident, so untested cold-entry is the default unless someone deliberately adds that test path.

Finally, for anything auth-gated, I'd want an explicit answer for what happens if the link arrives while the user is logged out: queue-and-resume after login is the pattern I'd push for, rather than either discarding the link or navigating into a screen with no valid session.

**Testing:** whether you can turn "deep links are risky" into a concrete, repeatable review checklist rather than a vague awareness.
